questions.prompt: Why can't word embeddings on their own tell the two meanings of "bank" apart?
options: Because "bank" isn't in their vocabulary
Because they give "bank" the same list of numbers in every sentence
Because they only work for Hindi words
Because embeddings can't store more than one word
questions.explanation: A word embedding is looked up from a table, so "bank" gets the same numbers whether it's by the Ganga or where you pay your fees. A Transformer updates each token's numbers using the tokens around it.

questions.prompt: Why does a Transformer add position information to each token?
options: To make the text shorter
To count how many tokens the prompt has
Because it reads all the tokens together, so it wouldn't otherwise know their order
To translate the text into another language
questions.explanation: A Transformer handles all the tokens of a prompt together, not one after another. Without position information, "Dog bites man" and "Man bites dog" would look the same to it.

questions.prompt: In attention, what is a token's query?
options: What the token is looking for in the other tokens
The information it passes on to other tokens
Its ID number in the vocabulary
The question the user typed
questions.explanation: Each token's query is compared with the other tokens' keys (what they can offer). Good matches get more attention, and the token takes in a mix of their values (the information they pass on).

questions.prompt: In GPT-2, the token "it" in "...because it was too heavy" is being processed. Which tokens can it look at?
options: Every token, including "heavy"
Only "heavy"
Only the token just before it
Itself and the tokens before it, but not "was", "too" or "heavy"
questions.explanation: In GPT-style models a token can only look at itself and earlier tokens, because the model's job is to predict what comes next. So at "it", GPT-2 hasn't seen "heavy" yet.

questions.prompt: In the real GPT-2 head from this lesson, where does "it" in "...lift the suitcase because it was too heavy" put the most attention, apart from the first word?
options: On "suitcase"
On "Riya"
On "because"
It spreads its attention equally over every token
questions.explanation: That head sends 52.4% of the attention from "it" to "suitcase". With "she" in the same place, the same head sends 31.5% to "Riya" instead. Nobody programmed this: it came out of training.

questions.prompt: What does the feed-forward network in each Transformer block do?
options: It decides which token to pick next
It splits the text into tokens
It works on each token's numbers on their own, like the small neural network in lesson 9
It sends each token's numbers to every other token
questions.explanation: After attention mixes information between tokens, the feed-forward network works on each token separately. In GPT-2 these networks hold about two-thirds of the parameters in each block.

questions.prompt: Your prompt doubles in length, from 1,000 tokens to 2,000. Roughly how much more work does each attention head do?
options: The same amount
About twice as much
About four times as much
About ten times as much
questions.explanation: Every token compares itself with every token before it: 1,000 tokens make 500,500 comparisons, and 2,000 make 2,001,000. Doubling the text roughly quadruples the work, one reason long prompts cost more.

questions.prompt: A team wants to train a language model quickly on thousands of GPUs. Why would they choose a Transformer over an older model that reads one word at a time?
options: Transformers don't need any training data
A Transformer handles all the tokens together, so training can do many calculations at once on GPUs
Transformers never make mistakes
Older models can't run on computers at all
questions.explanation: Reading one word at a time means each step waits for the last. A Transformer handles the whole text together, which suits GPUs: its authors found it "more parallelizable", needing "significantly less time to train". That's a big reason it took over.
